tips.title: Write the place values down first
tips.body: Every binary conversion starts the same way: **128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1**. Write that row before anything else and the rest is adding up. Trying to hold the doubling in your head is where mistakes come from.

tips.title: One hex digit is exactly four bits
tips.body: To go from binary to hex, **split into fours from the right** and convert each half on its own: `1001 1100` is 9 and 12, so **9C**. No division needed in either direction.

tips.title: AQA uses 1 kB = 1,000 bytes
tips.body: The specification lists the **decimal** prefixes: 1 kB is **1,000** bytes, 1 MB is 1,000 kB, and so on. You may have seen 1,024 elsewhere — that is the older powers-of-two usage, and the specification says you do not need it.

tips.title: Eight bits stop at 255
tips.body: The largest 8-bit value is **11111111 = 255 = FF**. If a conversion gives you more than 255 from eight bits, or more than two hex digits, something has gone wrong — check it before moving on.

tips.title: b is a bit, B is a byte
tips.body: The specification is explicit: lower case **b** means a **bit**, capital **B** means a **byte**. So 8 b = 1 B, and a "100 Mb" connection is eight times slower than a "100 MB" one sounds.

why.matters:
A computer has no way to store a letter, a colour or a sound. It has switches that are **on or off**, and everything else is a decision about how to write something real as those switches.

That is why this topic comes first. Binary is not a quirky way of counting — it is the only thing the hardware can do, and every file size, every limit and every "unsupported character" further on is a consequence of the encoding somebody chose.

examples.title: Why a photo is bigger than a message
examples.body:
A text message of 160 characters stores **one byte a character**: about 160 bytes. A photograph stores **three bytes a pixel**, and there are 4000 × 3000 of them — **36 MB**.

The file sizes are not arbitrary and they are not a property of photographs. They follow from what is being written down: a few hundred characters against twelve million colour values. Once you can count what a file contains, you can predict its size before you save it.

props.caption: Drawn to true proportion. The message is there.

visual.alt: Two bars drawn to true proportion: a thirty-six megabyte photograph against a one hundred and sixty byte text message, which is too small to see at the same scale

examples.title: Why a scan of a page is bigger than the page
examples.body:
Type a page and it is about 3000 characters — **3000 bytes**. Scan the same page and it is **26 MB**, about **8,700 times** as much, and it says exactly the same thing.

The scanner has no idea there are letters in the image. It is storing **colours**, so it records the white paper as carefully as the ink, pixel by pixel. That is also why a scanned page cannot be searched until software has looked at the picture and worked out what the letters were.

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion for the same page of words: twenty-six megabytes when scanned as an image against three kilobytes when typed as characters

examples.title: Why the phone says 128 GB and you have less
examples.body:
The specification is explicit about the prefixes, and so is the industry that sells you the storage: **1 kB = 1,000 B**, and a megabyte is 1,000 of those. A "128 GB" phone holds 128 **billion** bytes.

Some operating systems then report that space using 1024 instead of 1,000 at every step, so the same chip reads as about 119. Nothing is missing and nobody is cheating; two conventions are being used for one number. AQA asks for the decimal one, which is also what is printed on the box.

visual.alt: A table of the units of information: a bit is a single nought or one, a byte is eight bits, a kilobyte is a thousand bytes and a megabyte is a thousand kilobytes, using the decimal prefixes the specification gives

steps.title: Three number bases
steps.body:
**A base is how many digits a number system has.**

- **Decimal, base 10** — ten digits, 0 to 9. What people count in.
- **Binary, base 2** — two digits, 0 and 1. What computers use.
- **Hexadecimal, base 16** — sixteen digits: 0 to 9, then **A B C D E F** standing for 10 to 15.

**Computers use binary to represent all data and instructions.** A circuit is easiest to build with two reliable states — on and off, high and low voltage — so everything is stored as patterns of two symbols.

**A bit pattern on its own means nothing.** The same eight bits could be a whole number, a letter, part of a colour in a photograph, part of a sound, or an instruction. What it means depends entirely on what the computer has been told to do with it. This is worth holding on to, because the rest of this unit is really about the different things one pattern can be read as.

**Why hexadecimal is used** is asked directly on the paper. Hex is not a different way of storing anything — nothing is ever stored in hex. It is a way of **writing** binary for people:

- It is much **shorter**: `10011100` becomes `9C`.
- It is easier to **read, remember and copy**, so people make **fewer mistakes**.
- One hex digit is exactly **four bits**, so converting is quick and nothing is lost.

Colour codes on web pages are written in hex for exactly this reason.

check.prompt: Why is hexadecimal often used in computer science?
options: It is a shorter way to write binary, so people make fewer mistakes
Computers store data in hexadecimal rather than in binary
It can represent numbers that binary cannot represent
It takes up less space in memory than binary does
check.solution: Hex is **for people**, not for the machine. It is shorter and easier to read and copy, so fewer mistakes are made. Everything is still **stored in binary** — hex takes up no less space.

steps.title: Binary and decimal
steps.body:
**Each binary place is worth twice the one to its right.** For eight bits:

**128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1**

**Binary to decimal: add up the places with a 1 under them.** For `10011100`, the 1s sit under 128, 16, 8, 4, and 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = **156**.

**Decimal to binary: work left to right, taking each place if it fits.** For 156: 128 fits, leaving 28. 64 does not fit, so 0. 32 does not, so 0. 16 fits, leaving 12. 8 fits, leaving 4. 4 fits, leaving 0. Then 2 and 1 are both 0. That gives `10011100`.

**The specification sets the range at 0 to 255.** Eight bits, and 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. So:

- the largest value is `11111111` = **255**
- an answer above 255 from eight bits is **wrong**

**Pad to eight bits.** 45 is `00101101`, not `101101`. The leading zeros carry no value but they show you are working in a byte, and questions usually expect them.

steps.title: Units of information
steps.body:
**The two units the specification names:**

- A **bit** is the **fundamental unit of information** — a single 0 or 1.
- A **byte** is a group of **8 bits**.

And the symbols matter: **`b` is a bit, `B` is a byte.** A broadband speed quoted as 100 Mb is not the same as 100 MB.

**Larger quantities use prefixes, and AQA uses the decimal ones:**

| Prefix | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **kilo (kB)** | 1 kB = **1,000** bytes |
| **mega (MB)** | 1 MB = **1,000** kilobytes |
| **giga (GB)** | 1 GB = **1,000** megabytes |
| **tera (TB)** | 1 TB = **1,000** gigabytes |

Each step is **×1,000**, so 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes and 1 GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes.

**You may have seen 1,024 instead.** Historically these words were used for powers of 2, and 2¹⁰ = 1,024. The specification notes this but says the **decimal** values are what you use, and that you do not need the kibi/mebi names that properly belong to the powers of 2.

**Comparing sizes is the skill being tested.** To see how many 5 MB photos fit in 4 GB, put both in the same unit: 4 GB = 4000 MB, and 4000 ÷ 5 = **800** photos.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Write the place values first, every time.** `128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1`. Doubling in your head is an easy way to slip a place.

**Split into groups of four bits from the right, not the left.** Binary to hex works because one hex digit is exactly four bits. With an odd number of bits, pad on the **left**: `1011010` is seven bits, so it becomes `01011010` = 5A. Splitting from the left instead gives a different and wrong answer.

**Know that 255 = 11111111 = FF is the ceiling.** It is a free check on every answer. More than 255 from a byte, or three hex digits, means something is wrong.

**Hex is a notation, not a storage format.** *It takes up less space* is a common answer and it is wrong: the machine stores binary either way. Hex is shorter **to write and read**, which is a benefit to **people**, and that is the reason to give.

**Use AQA's decimal prefixes.** 1 kB = **1,000** bytes. You will meet 1,024 elsewhere, and it is not wrong in the world — but the specification names the decimal values, and a calculation built on 1,024 will not give the answer the question expects.

**Convert to a common unit before comparing.** Do not try to divide gigabytes by megabytes in your head. Put both into MB, or both into bytes, and the division becomes ordinary arithmetic.

**Remember that a bit pattern has no meaning by itself.** `10011100` is 156 as a whole number, but the same eight bits could be a character, part of a pixel's colour, or part of a sound sample.

**Watch the case of b and B.** A 100 Mb/s connection transfers 12.5 MB each second, not 100. Exam questions do use both.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Three bases: **decimal (10)**, **binary (2)**, **hexadecimal (16)**.
- Hex digits run 0 to 9 then **A to F** for 10 to 15.
- Computers use **binary for all data and instructions**.
- A bit pattern has **no meaning on its own** — it depends on how it is read.
- **Hex is used because it is shorter for people**, not because it saves space.
- Eight-bit place values: **128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1**.
- **Binary to decimal**: add the places with a 1 under them.
- **Decimal to binary**: take each place left to right if it fits.
- The range is **0 to 255**: `11111111` = 255 = **FF**.
- **One hex digit = four bits**; split into fours **from the right**.
- `10011100` = 156 = **9C**.
- A **bit** is the fundamental unit; a **byte** is **8 bits**.
- **b** is a bit, **B** is a byte.
- Prefixes are **decimal**: 1 kB = **1,000** B, and each step up is ×1,000.
- To compare sizes, **convert both to the same unit** first.

questions.prompt: Explain how binary, decimal and hexadecimal relate to one another, and why hexadecimal is often used in computer science.
questions.solution:
**Decimal** is **base 10** and uses the digits 0 to 9; it is what people count in. **Binary** is **base 2** and uses only 0 and 1; computers use it to represent **all data and instructions**, because a circuit is easiest to build with two reliable states. **Hexadecimal** is **base 16**, using 0 to 9 and then **A to F** for the values 10 to 15.

The important relationship is between **binary and hexadecimal**. Sixteen is $2^4$, so **one hex digit is exactly four bits**. That means the two can be converted a block at a time, each block of four bits on its own: `10011100` splits from the right into `1001` and `1100`, which are 9 and 12, so the value is **9C**. Going back is just as direct. Nothing is lost or rounded in either direction.

Decimal has no such relationship with binary, because 10 is **not** a power of 2. No group of bits lines up with a decimal digit, so converting has to be done by adding place values: `10011100` is $128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 156$.

**Hexadecimal is used** because it is a much **shorter** way of writing binary — two characters instead of eight for a single byte — and because it is far easier for a person to **read, remember and copy** without slipping a digit. Long runs of 0s and 1s are exactly the kind of thing people make mistakes with. Since the conversion to and from binary is so direct, none of that convenience costs anything. This is why colour codes on web pages are written in hex.

It is worth saying clearly what hexadecimal is **not**. It is **not a storage format**: the computer holds binary whatever notation a person writes it in, so hex does **not** save any memory. A common wrong answer is that hex "takes up less space". The saving is on the page and in the reader's attention, not in the machine.

questions.prompt: A phone has 64 GB of storage. Photos are 5 MB each and songs are 4 MB each. Explain how you would work out how many of each it could hold, and explain the units involved.
questions.solution:
First, the **units**. A **bit** is the fundamental unit of information, a single 0 or 1, and a **byte** is a group of **8 bits**. Larger quantities use prefixes, and the specification uses the **decimal** ones: 1 **kB** is 1,000 bytes, 1 **MB** is 1,000 kB, and 1 **GB** is 1,000 MB. Each step up is a factor of 1,000, so 64 GB is $64 \times 1000 = 64\,000$ MB.

The symbols matter too: lower case **b** means a bit and capital **B** means a byte, so a figure quoted in Mb is eight times less data than the same figure in MB.

To work out the **number of photos**, both quantities must be in the **same unit** first — dividing gigabytes by megabytes directly is an easy way to go wrong. With the storage in MB:

$64\,000 \div 5 = \mathbf{12\,800}$ photos.

For **songs** at 4 MB each:

$64\,000 \div 4 = \mathbf{16\,000}$ songs.

The phone could hold either of those, or some mixture, but not both totals at once — the 64 GB is shared.

There are **assumptions** worth stating. The calculation treats the whole 64 GB as free, which it never is: the operating system and the apps take a substantial share, so the real figures would be lower. It also assumes every photo is exactly 5 MB, when in practice photo sizes vary a great deal with the subject and the compression used, so 12,800 is an estimate rather than a count.

Finally, the **1,000 against 1,024** question. The specification uses the decimal prefixes, so 1 GB is 1,000 MB and that is what an exam answer should use. Historically these words were often used for powers of 2, where $2^{10} = 1024$, and some manufacturers and operating systems still count that way — which is why a drive sold as 64 GB can show as around 59.6 GB on a computer. The specification notes this history but says the **kibi** and **mebi** names that properly belong to the powers of 2 are not required, and a calculation built on 1,024 will not give the answer the question expects.

questions.prompt: Convert the decimal number 200 to hexadecimal.
questions.solution: 200 is $128 + 64 + 8$, so in binary it is `11001000`. Split into fours: `1100` is 12, which is **C**, and `1000` is 8. So **C8**. Check: $12 \times 16 = 192$, plus 8 is 200 ✓

questions.prompt: Convert the hexadecimal number 3F to binary, using eight bits.
questions.solution: Each hex digit becomes four bits. 3 is `0011`, and F is 15, which is `1111`. So **00111111**. Check: $3 \times 16 + 15 = 63$, and $32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 63$ ✓

questions.prompt: A 2 TB drive is filled with video files of 500 MB each. Using the decimal prefixes in the specification, how many files does it hold?
questions.solution: TB and MB are two prefixes apart, so convert one step at a time: 2 TB is $2 \times 1000 = 2000$ GB, and 2000 GB is $2000 \times 1000 = 2\,000\,000$ MB. Then $2\,000\,000 \div 500 = $ **4000** files. Converting only one step, to 2000 GB, and dividing by 500 would give 4, which is far too few.

examTechnique.body:
Write the place values **128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1** before any conversion. For hex, split into fours **from the right**, padding with zeros on the left if needed.

Use AQA's **decimal** prefixes — 1 kB = 1,000 B — and convert both quantities to the **same unit** before comparing. Check every byte answer against the ceiling: **11111111 = 255 = FF**.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the **place values down first** and checks its own conversion by adding back. It splits into groups of four bits **from the right** and pads short numbers on the left. It explains hex as shorter **for people**, and says explicitly that nothing is stored in it. It uses **1 kB = 1,000 B**, converts to a common unit before comparing, and knows the ceiling **11111111 = 255 = FF** as a free check. It can also say why binary and hex convert so cleanly — **16 is a power of 2** — while decimal does not, and that a bit pattern means nothing until something decides how to read it.
